The thrust towards industry and construction 4.0 has ushered in the penetration of robotic systems, improving production efficiency while maintaining high-quality standards.
Robotic systems are sophisticated and heterogeneous architectures incorporating many diverse sensors, actuating systems, hardware and software components, applications, interfaces, etc.
For this competition, we will only focus on attacks that could compromise the operation of a robot performing monitoring tasks within a construction facility.

In more detail, the data that we are concerned about can be divided into three categories: i) data-in-transit, ii) data-at-rest, and iii) data-in-use. The security risks and the impacts of attacks targeting each data subcategory as well as the methodologies that need to be applied to ensure that the data have not been altered are different. Attackers could compromise data during their collection stage, i.e., data-in-use.
These data can be information collected from robot sensors. By spoofing these sensors, the situational awareness of the robot can be compromised.
Attacks against lidar, gyroscopes, and accelerometers have been reported.
Modifying the sensor readings can affect its movement, or make the robot operate uncontrollably.
Attacks against camera systems and machine learning-based algorithms have also been reported.

Some examples include blinding attacks, which have been shown to have catastrophic impacts on autonomous vehicles. Similarly for our robot, such attacks could either affect its awareness of potential obstacles or hide objects impairing its monitoring objective.
Data-in-transit could be another attack entry point.

Attacks such as communication jamming and spoofing, replay, man-in-the-middle, and DoS could compromise the objectives of our system by altering or limiting the availability of the data-in-transit to their intended receiving ends.

Furthermore, the lack of authentication, authorizations, and attestation schemes could allow adversaries to gain access, modify control commands, or even send malicious commands  Ò in the case of insecure/unencrypted communication protocols - to the agent itself, jeopardizing not only the robot's operation, but the entire construction infrastructure.
Data-at-rest could also become a security vulnerability for our system.
Data could be located on the robot itself and on the external computer and the HMI.
Modifying, encrypting, or deleting such data could have significant impacts on the facility's operation.

Such attacks include ransomware, trojan, wiper, and rootkit attacks. Attackers could exploit lack of secure storage modules, redundancy schemes, integrity checks, secure firmware updates and boot partitions, stack/heap-based buffer overflows, non-executable memory, and in general host-based defenses and weaponize the robotic agent.
The description of the robotic system provided in the challenge consists of multiple and interconnected levels. At the lowest level of the robot stack, we have its physical components.
An attacker with physical access to the device could impair the navigation, localization, and monitoring objectives of the robotic system by directly attacking it.

For instance, the firmware used for the coordination of the controllers could be flashed, modified, or erased. In the case of firmware modification attacks, the adversaries could stealthily hide their attacks and perform anomalous operations sparingly. Especially in the case of process-aware attacks carefully planting minor modifications can maximize the attack impact while the robotic agent might be operating in an indistinguishable-from-normal fashion.
Levels 1 through 4 of the robotic stack encapsulate its core computational and communication infrastructure.
As a result, attacks can be classified into two categories, i) attacks targeting the embedded device itself and ii) attacks aimed at the communicated information.
For the first category, different types of vulnerabilities potentially existing in the RPi 4 device and the operating system running on TurtleBot3 could be exploited.
For instance, heap- or stack-based buffer overflow attacks can compromise the agent allowing random command execution and privilege escalation.

Unencrypted storage media could be compromised and critical information, such as alarms and control limits can be overridden. If authentication and authorization policies are not enforced and users can perform commands, using admin privileges, attackers might be able to erase critical memory partitions handling the interaction with external sensors, its imaging capabilities (e.g., erase camera drivers), or impair its network processes (e.g., network drivers).

Such destructive attacks could render the robot uncontrollable or unreachable (DoS). Lack of secure boot and/or secure firmware updates could allow the deployment of counterfeit software on the robotic agent allowing attacker persistence (e.g., advanced persistent threats) or the installation of backdoors enabling remote privileged access to the device by unauthorized users.
The second category includes the attack classes that can be carried out over the communication channels.

Man-in-the-middle attacks could be performed to intercept, scan/sniff packets to obtain information and/or modify their content, especially if encryption and authentication mechanisms are not enforced.
Wireless jamming and DoS attacks could also be performed by flooding the communication medium, i.e., wireless channels.
In the case of mission critical systems delays might not be allowed due to real-time operational constraints.
Furthermore, in the case of manual control of the robot, packet spoofing attacks could be implemented to misguide the robot or maliciously control it.

The manipulation of the robot can be either performed using wired media or via remote access to it. To reprogram the robotic agent via a wired connection, we first need to determine the environment where the robot is operating.

If the robot operates in a supervised environment, then the attacker will require physical access to it. Connecting external wired devices to an operational robot could raise suspicion and result in the easy detection of a potential compromise. However, if the robot is not monitored an attacker with physical access to it, i.e., insider threat, could tamper with its firmware maliciously impacting the robot's control objectives (e.g., autonomous operation) and its overall performance.
As a result, both the process automation environment as well as the personnel safety could be jeopardized.

Remote manipulation, in turn, can be divided into, i) manipulation of the robot itself, or ii) indirect manipulation of the robot by restricting the CPS environment in which the robot operates. The robot system is designed to interact with an external computer, via a router, which can send control commands to the robot, meaning that if the external computer gets compromised, attackers can send malicious commands affecting the robot's state. If these commands are executed without any authentication and authorization of the party that issues them the robot could be instructed to perform malicious tasks.

On the other hand, the router as a connection medium can also be another attack entry point. If an attacker gain control of the router, she/he could modify the data received and sent over the router, with potentially serious consequences.

For example, the robot operates in an industrial environment where receiving real-time and accurate information about its surroundings is crucial. Compromising the accuracy of the sensed information or even the timely delivery of sensor updates could have destructive implications on the robot operation. If the sensors on the robotic agents are not well coordinated, an attacker would be able to target just one of them and affect the operation of the entire robot. For example, an attacker could place mirrors in the industrial environment rendering the LIDAR or camera-based navigation features of the robot unusable. Similarly, by compromising the robot's gyroscope, IMU or other sensors we could severely inhibit its localization accuracy and sabotage its autonomous operation. Finally, combined attacks could disrupt the robot's operational state (by targeting its sensors) and at the same time sending false control commands over the compromised router. Although such attacks require that the adversary has infiltrated both the physical and the cyber perimeter of the industrial environment, their impacts could be devastating.
It will be our objective as ethical hackers and cybersecurity researchers to first identify such vulnerabilities and then safeguard the robotic agent against adversarial attacks.

Once physical access to the robot is attained, the attacker could modify the robot's control logic. However, to successfully plant such control logic modification attacks the adversary needs to directly contact the robot, and then modify the robotic agent's logic in such a way that will not make the robot inoperative. Therefore, to defend against such types of attacks we first need to eliminate the access of unauthorized personnel to the robot, and second to prohibit firmware modifications unless security policies and protocols are followed.
Further, we can use camera surveillance, or equip it with a GPS transmitter while using geo-location/fencing policies.

If the robot deviates from the predefined construction site areas, alerts can be issued to the system operators. Physical security countermeasures can also be enforced limiting the access to the robot to only authorized personnel and increasing the difficulty for attackers to achieve persistence within the CPS environment. Another security countermeasure could be to make the firmware immutable after the robot has been deployed and disabling over-the-air updates. Secure firmware updates could be allowed under closely monitored and regulated circumstances.
Furthermore, any debugging interfaces on the robot itself should be disabled ensuring that no information about the operational semantics can be leaked.
Host-based defense mechanisms such as firmware encryption, obfuscation and signing could also be enforced to deter adversaries even if they can manage to get access to the device's firmware.
The most vulnerable component of this framework is the router, used to connect the robot master computer to the external network.
The router uses Wi-Fi, which widens the threat surface of our setup. Many successful attack methodologies against Wi-Fi communications have been reported.
Granted that the robot is equipped with an encryption chip, SSL transmission can be realized, that is, all data packets are encrypted and can resist replay attacks.

Even though, replay attacks can be avoided, attackers could use jamming attacks to block Wi-Fi signals (DoS attacks), fake or redirect in-transit data, or decrypt and analyze captured packets to exfiltrate sensitive information or craft malicious payloads.
A potential improvement could be to abandon the use of Wi-Fi and use another non-TCP/IP protocol, such as ZigBee or Bluetooth.
By changing Wi-Fi to other wireless protocols, and using an additional protocol conversion gateway, external hosts connect to the robot through the gateway.

As a result, another level of security is added to deter attackers. To defend against external attackers, traditional network security countermeasures can be used. Such defenses include, subnet isolation, deployment of firewalls, DMZ, IDS/IPS, etc.
The robot will be used in mission-critical industrial environments such as construction.

Malware attacks have been gaining popularity, especially in such CPS environments due to their acute consequences on the undelaying infrastructures. In more detail, malware can disrupt processes resulting in asset damage or financial losses.
Furthermore, these processes are occurring in real-time, so their effects can be immediate, endangering both the operations and the safety of the involved personnel.
As cybersecurity researchers, we are naturally curious and motivated to understand the effects of compromising any of the layers of the robotic stack depicted in Fig.
as well as their impacts on the environment.
Unveiling these effects could help us identify the best attack scenarios from the attacker's perspective.
Then we can optimally allocate security resources and prioritize them to mitigate the most serious attacks.
By identifying vulnerabilities within the code, the team can put into practice their critical thinking and creativity.
For example, attackers could try to reduce the movement speed of the robot, delay important processes, or alter the robot's control logic to permanently damage its actuators.

Therefore, detection can be implemented with a supplemental layer of security, on the host device, via segregating the critical components and processes or providing redundancy to them. Furthermore, host-based defenses can help in recognizing stealthy attacks that can affect components such as the wheels, camera sensors, or motors.

As a result, effective detection strategies can be devised, to notify the robot of anomalies and initiate corrective actions to prevent or minimize damages. Such strategies could leverage feedback systems that inform both the robot and operators of such anomalies.
Another motivation is understanding the diverse effects of the different types of attacks and what is the most disruptive attack with minimal effort from the attacker's side.
Given the interoperable robotic architecture that we will be dealing with, each attack type might require different detection techniques and penetration procedures.

For instance, it is important for an attacker to know which is easier: reaching the levels remotely via the Wi-Fi router and changing the settings of the components, e.g., actuator thresholds, or directly attacking the sensors.
The existing detection techniques' efficacy would be monitored for each attack on the robot such as alarm triggering or stopping the current process when a certain threshold is detected.
The biggest incentive, however, is the sense of achievement in finding diverse pathways to ethically disrupt critical tasks and then protect industrial processes.

Wi-Fi Communication Module: Implement the latest Wi-Fi security protocols (WPA3) to address vulnerabilities in the Wi-Fi module. WPA3 replaces the PSK method used in WPA2 with SAE, also known as Dragonfly.
This change enhances the security of the Wi-Fi network.
SAE doesn't rely on static pre-shared keys or passwords, which can be vulnerable to dictionary attacks.
Instead, it uses a stronger method based on the Diffie-Hellman key exchange protocol.
This means that even if an attacker captures the encrypted handshake, they cannot easily launch offline dictionary attacks to guess the password.
SAE allows both the client and the access point (Wi-Fi router) to mutually authenticate each other during the key exchange process.

Another feature of enhanced encryption in WPA3 is forward secrecy. Forward secrecy ensures that past sessions' encryption keys are not compromised if the long-term secret (password or pre-shared key) is ever discovered.

Application Layer Firewall: Deploy an application-layer firewall that inspects network traffic at the application level.

Default Deny Rule: Configure your firewall with a default deny rule.
This means that all traffic is denied by default unless explicitly allowed.
